title: Repositioning
text: A long day repositioning from Maine Yacht Center, Portland to Salem, MA. We were off the dock by 0430 and motoring through dense fog until it broke about 1000.  Got to try the new code sail for a bit and mixed the day up with some sailing and motor sailing.  The winds were all over the place but always on our bow.  Glad to be back on the home mooring.

title: Sea trials
text: Out and back and around Salem, Manchester, and Marblehead. We spent a while in 25-32kt winds running the new jib through its paces, tuning the inner forestay and runners to match.  It’s a really nice upgrade from the excellent but blown out North 3Di. It’s got a higher clew which is great for seeing lobster pots and broader shoulders giving us a lot of options with car position.

title: Pen Bay transit
text: Mostly motoring with almost no wind transiting Pen Bay through the middle of North Haven and Vinalhaven. Cold but sunny and enoug pots that I'm really ready for a break from northern new england.  Free mooring at Safe Harbor Rockland, the cleanest and friendliest place in Maine (alright Hinckley is tied for first).

title: Overnight to Somes Sound, MDI
text: Overnight run to MDI.  It was a nice overnight broad reach but died at sunrise once Cadillac and pots came into view

title: Pen Bay to home
text: Rough passage.  It was left over rollers that really threw us all over the boat.  Without much wind we were just motor sailing back to Cape Ann for sunrise and there was really no sleep for either of us. The commercial shipping lanes in and out of Portland and Porthsmouth were strangely busy so lots to monitor on AIS and radar. One of the funniest exchanges on VHF was recorded for those looking for the ultimate North Shore accent.  We arrive late morning to our mooring and after to relax a bit before driving home.  We were both weaving while walking for the next 24 hours.

title: Marella and friends
text: Marella, Michelle, and Nina got to enjoy the sun and Doug got to have a relaxing sail around Salem Harbor.

title: Salem to Provincetown and a whale
text: Got a 0745 start and a cold but wicked fast day sailing to P-Town.  We made a steady 8.5kts on a broad reach carrying the full main and code in 14-16 kites.  The waves picked up as we got closer to the destination making sure we were swing a lot once we got to the anchorage.  The Spade anchor set the second it hit the bottom but with quits overnight we left 5:1 including the snubber.  The exciting part is we nearly hit a right wale (we have video to prove) and I het to divert course and lay on the horn to avoid a collision.

title: PTown to Sandwich
text: Pretty quiet day across Cape Cod bay to time the channel pretty well.  We topped off on fuel at $5.99 a gallon (40 gallons) and got 1.2 gallons of gas in the jerry can for the dinghy. The slips in Sandwich are always crazy tight but this worked out fine.  Marella and I ate at Seafood Sam's for dinner at the recommendation of the fuel dock manager.  It was a good call but really rich.  Too many beers might have been the problem too, who knows. I ordered a new macerator pump before our trip South because no head would be a bad thing.

title: Edgartown to Cuttyhunk
text: Cool, sunny, and current filled day of sailign when we could and motoring the rest.  We needed to get to Cuttyhunk in time to get in a hike and stretch legs before nighfall. It was a fun location - smalled town by population in Massachusetts.  Saw it all in 45 minutes. Moorings were tight but people were nice and there is a raw bar that you can hail on channel 71 who will rock up with fresh seafood.

title: Sandwich to Edgartown
text: A reasonable 8am start from Sandwich to time the canal right.  We ended up going down Buzzards Bay under jib so as not to get to Wood's Hole until the current switched and even then we had to sail about at the entrace for an hour or two.  We were hailed by Steve Ricci from Pouchy who had just come from Hadley Harbor which was not even a location I knew - better place to hang for the hour or night.  It was a white knuckle run though Broadway at Woods Hole but I've done it enough it was fine.  As soon as we were through we were hailed by another boat still back in Buzzards Bay looking for a PIREP on current conditions.  Honestly, and don't tell anyone, but Vineyard Sound is a lousy sailing location.  Shoals everywhere, silly currents and Steamship Authority vessels all over the place.  We managed to broad reach to the entrance of Edgartown and settle in to mooring 32.  Dang do I love Edgartown.

title: Cuttyhunk to Provincetown
text: Full on day.  We left the second we could see where we were going.  The engine was warming up and coffe ready by 0530 and we cast off by 0545.  A nauseating motor back out the narrow channel into Buzzards Bay and we absolutely rockets up Buzzards Bay on a broad reach making 9kts in 12-15 kts of wind under a full main and the code zero.  We hit the channel just as the current was building around 9am, flew through about 11kts SOG and popped out into Cape Cod Bay as the line of torrential rain let loose.  We were prepared but it was spicy.  The most amazing Furuno radar finally just got lost in a wall of water - 3" per hour.  Rather than anchor I got us a mooring at Provincetown Marina which was mostly for peace of mind.  They were very nice but Marella and I never left the saloon choosing instead to sip a cocktail and play (learning) cribbage.

title: Provincetown to Salem - force 6-7
text:
Oh boy, what a sail 😳.  We again left at 0545 from Provincetown Marina, motored to the outer lighthouse and shook out the jib and a half main.  The wind was building and the angle was terrible.  Everything was lining up to prevent progress home.  We took a tack almost due north out to Stellwagen Bank leaving us about 20nm off Boston Harbor, tacked to what should have been Nahant but by the time we get 5 miles from shore turned into Scituate.  We motored most of the way home concerned we'd run out of daylight.  The waves were really the problem at 4-5 but 3.5-4 seconds and from two separate angles.  Ardenna got slammed but the windshield and dodger kept us dry.  No going down below for about four hours until we got close enough to shore the fetch shortened the chop.  

"Pan-pan pan-pan pan-pan this is the United States Coast Guard Sector Boston.  For a marine safety broadcast regarding a small craft advisory in the advisory location tune to channel 22A. Break.  This is the United States Coast Guard Sector Boston, out."  

Yeah, thanks, we're FULLY aware.

title: Salem to Quincy repositioning
text: Aviva and I repositioned Ardenna to Marina Bay, Quincy (https://safeharbor.com/locations/safe-harbor-marina-bay/) in preparation for a DR departure later in the week.  It was a beautiful day although cold but unfortunately the 7-8 knots was right on the nose so it was mostly motoring. When we got to Marina Bay we went straight to the fuel dock where only the high speed pump was working.  Even with Aviva's help in calling out the gallons from the pump I made a hell of a mess.  I think we eventually went through a dozen fuel pads to clean it up and some even came out the port side deck vent.  Once wiped down it was a quick reverse into the face dock right across from our old slip, D39.

title: Day 2 - Weather routers and a change of plans
text: It’s an amazing day of sailing with jib and full main flying in 18-20kts averaging 8.2-8.5kts.  Everyone’s seasickness is gone and we’re starting to get into a crew groove.  For this trip we’ve hired a weather routers to support high level decision-making.  It’s especially helpful when you’re tired and felling a bit snow blind.  This morning I asked for an updated point of view on getting from our current position to Samaná and quickly decided to bail out for a day or two in Bermuda.  There is a big trough at 31N and a tropical storm forming in South Florida that is going to barrel up the coast so if we outrun it, and we probably would, then happy days.  If not, gale force winds, thunderstorms, etc.  Tonight we cross the Gulf Stream and then head to Bermuda.  Glad I still have the courtesy flag.

title: Day 3 - Halloween ghosts as we cross the Gulfstream
text:
It was a physically taxing day as we entered the Gulfstream overnight before the moon rose and experienced the power of wind and current together.  We have carefully planned with our weather router the entry point and timing but it was still, as Mike said, ‘full on.’  We had a nice day of sailing a broad reach with winds 20-25g30 under full main and jib (a 103).  The waves really were 8-10 with plenty of 12’ but the period was manageable.  The current was at just enough of an angle at we all found every hand hold in the boat.  James and Kathy reported 13.1kts on the back of a wave and Mike yelled out 14.2kts.  Ardenna is loving this and happy to chew up miles.  We set a boat record yesterday 217 miles in 24 hours.  

The crew is doing great.  Jake’s and Kathy are ready for their own Contest and Mike would rather hang out in the cockpit and take it all in.  Next stop Bermuda.

title: Day 1 - It’s on!
text: Day one and we’re on our way.  We left the dock exactly at 0700 and motored out through Boston Harbor entering the Bay the long way (it was very low, low tide). From there we set a line to Provincetown making 8.4 - 8.8 knots on a broad reach in 18-22kts true.  Along the way we dodged lobster pots and then dodged some more and saw whales. Cape Cod is really amazing and never gets old.  It was a happy day of hanging out together in the cockpit and getting acquainted with Ardenna.  She’s in her element on long passages. We’ve got a touch of early sea sickness going around but spirits are still high.  We’ve got to make time to cross the Gulf Stream in the wee hours of Saturday morning so it’s a bit of a grind.

title: Day 4 - the Gulf Stream payoff
text:
After a meal of tortellini and spicy red sauce last night, everyone seems to have gotten good sleep and found a watch rhythm. The morning started with a spectacular sunrise and not one of those giant suns peaking above the horizon deals but clouds at many layers and colors that you don’t really think exist in a paint store.  It was a two pot of coffee morning which kicked off a day of hanging out in the cockpit and enjoying some amazing sailing.  It was pretty much a steady 17-22kts on a broad reach under job then code.  After lunch it dropped to 12-14 so the gennaker went up and until a line squal was noticed by eagle eyed Mike and his trusty Furuno radar companion so it was lowered out of an abundance of caution.  Tonight’s meal was vegetarian and beef chilies over rice with tortilla chips.  

We’ll be in St George’s around sunrise to clear customs into Bermuda and head over to the Royal Hamilton Amateur Dinghy Club for a breakfast beer and shower.

title: Day 5 - Land Ho!
text:
The day started with a dark, dark night with 77 degree sea temps and 62 degree air.  It was cold and humid in the cockpit for watches and hot and humid below making for a lot of clothing changes. At this point in the journey the constant donning and removal of lifejackets and tethers is getting old and they’re leading to sore shoulders.  No choice but to endure for safety’s sake.  

We switched time zones some time after the Gulf Stream and then daylight saving made for some confusing watch schedules.  Twice Marella and Mike either did extended watches or showed up too early. At 2:30am Doug hailed Bermuda radio for permission to enter territorial waters and the very polite, BBC announcer sounding VHF operator, confirmed we are the 50’ blue sailboat Ardenna and granted approach to Town Cut.  About 6:30am we approached the safer water buoy and again hailed and were given permission to enter Convict Bay and drop anchor.  Once situated we hoisted the yellow quarantine flag, launched the dinghy, and motored in to clear customs on Ordnance Island.  

Clearance was fairly early but paper intensive with many signatures and stamping of papers.  Passports and exit papers in hand, we dinghyed back to the boat to start motoring to our home for the next few days, the Royal Hamilton Amateur Dinghy Club.   It’s looking like a Saturday afternoon or Sunday morning departure to Samaná so until then we are exploring Bermuda.
